title: Tom DeLay helped create TV ownership cap—he says Trump FCC has no authority to repeal it
gist: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has scheduled a Thursday vote, expected to pass 2-1, to repeal the statutory 39 percent national TV ownership cap and replace it with case-by-case merger review — and Tom DeLay, the Republican who negotiated the 39 percent figure into law in 2004, publicly says only Congress can change it. The legal fight is already teed up: Carr granted Nexstar a waiver to buy Tegna past 50 percent household reach, that integration is frozen by a judge in DirecTV's antitrust suit, and a pay-TV coalition says courts will quickly overturn the repeal.

themes.theme: The imminent vote and its market consequence

insights.claim: The FCC votes Thursday on Carr's proposal to repeal the 39 percent national audience reach cap and replace it with case-by-case review of each proposed merger, and the plan is likely to pass 2-1 with Carr and Republican Commissioner Olivia Trusty in favor.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A dated, near-certain regulatory event that unlocks a broadcast consolidation wave on paper; the real trade is in whether it survives judicial review, not in the vote itself.
insights.locator: The repeal plan is likely to pass 2–1 this week

insights.claim: Replacing a bright-line numerical cap with case-by-case merger review gives the FCC discretion to pick and choose which station groups get to expand, which the author links to Carr's goal of securing more positive news coverage for President Trump.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Discretionary approval converts M&A outcomes from a legal question into a political relationship, which changes how to handicap any individual broadcast deal.
insights.quote: This would make it easier for the FCC to pick and choose which station groups get to expand
insights.locator: The 39 percent cap has thus survived for over two decades

insights.claim: The 39 percent cap has survived for over two decades across four administrations, and Carr would be the first FCC chairman to actually test whether the agency can eliminate it entirely rather than merely assert the authority.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Two decades of chairmen declining to act on asserted authority is evidence prior counsel judged the legal risk too high — a caution flag on pricing in the repeal as durable.
insights.locator: Carr would be first to test whether FCC can kill cap

insights.claim: The sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, characterizes the repeal as an unlawful effort to hand control of the public airwaves to billionaire buddies of the administration, framing the dissent that a challenger would cite.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A written dissent laying out the statutory argument is the roadmap petitioners use on appeal; it raises the odds and speed of a stay.
insights.quote: The 39 percent cap is not an FCC rule that the commission can change on its own
insights.locator: Anna Gomez, the only Democrat on the FCC

themes.theme: Statutory history the courts will read

insights.claim: The cap's history runs FCC-set 25 percent in 1985, congressionally directed 35 percent in the Telecommunications Act of 1996, an FCC attempt at 45 percent in 2003, and a congressional override to 39 percent in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2004.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The one time an FCC raised the cap unilaterally, Congress reversed it within months — the precedent most relevant to forecasting the political response to Thursday's vote.
insights.locator: The TV ownership cap was originally implemented by the FCC

insights.claim: The 2004 law contains explicit text stating that the FCC's quadrennial obligation to repeal or modify regulations no longer in the public interest does not apply to any rules relating to the 39 percent national audience reach limitation.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: This is the operative statutory text a reviewing court will parse; the whole repeal turns on whether the carve-out only exempts the cap from quadrennial review or forbids changing it at all.
insights.quote: This subsection does not apply to any rules relating to the 39 percent national audience reach limitation in subsection (c)(1)(B).
insights.locator: During each quadrennial review

insights.claim: The 2004 law also barred the FCC from forbearing from applying telecom regulations to TV station owners exceeding the 39 percent limit, restrictive language absent from the 1996 statute.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The forbearance restriction is independent evidence Congress meant to bind the agency; it is the second textual hook challengers will use and one Carr's draft must explain away.
insights.locator: Another potential problem for Carr

insights.claim: The same 2004 budget provision also converted the FCC's media ownership reviews from biennial to quadrennial, meaning the cap restriction was part of a broader congressional effort to slow the agency's deregulatory cadence.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Context of intent matters in statutory interpretation; the surrounding provisions all point toward constraining, not empowering, the commission.
insights.locator: The budget bill changed the FCC’s biennial reviews to quadrennial

insights.claim: Tom DeLay, House majority leader from 2003 to 2005, published an op-ed in The Daily Wire arguing the FCC has no legal authority to repeal the cap because the 39 percent figure was specified by Congress rather than chosen by the commission.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Contemporaneous testimony from the deal's architect is unusually potent evidence of legislative intent and can be cited directly in briefs against the repeal.
insights.quote: Regulatory agencies cannot defy or modify laws enacted by Congress. If Chairman Carr wants to raise the statutory cap, he should ask Congress to pass a law giving him authority to do that.
insights.locator: I am a Republican

insights.claim: DeLay describes the 39 percent number as the product of a specific bargain with Sen. Ted Stevens: DeLay got the cap raised from Stevens's proposed 35 percent, and in exchange Stevens received certainty that the FCC could not raise it higher.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: If the number's entire purpose was purchasing agency-proof certainty, Carr's reading that the FCC retains discretion guts the consideration Congress bargained for — a strong intent argument for challengers.
insights.quote: My end of the deal was that the cap would be raised to 39 percent, and in return, Stevens received certainty that the FCC wouldn’t and couldn’t raise it higher.
insights.locator: In fact, I would have happily given the FCC authority

insights.claim: The 39 percent figure was reverse-engineered from existing corporate footprints: after the FCC raised the cap to 45 percent, CBS and Fox had acquired stations reaching nearly 39 percent of US households, and DeLay did not want to force divestitures of lawful purchases.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The cap was set to grandfather the largest incumbents of 2004 — evidence that the number was never a principled public-interest threshold, which cuts both ways in litigation.
insights.locator: After the FCC raised the cap to 45 percent

insights.claim: DeLay states he has sympathy for Carr's objectives and would have given the FCC authority over the cap in 2004 if Stevens had allowed it, making his opposition procedural rather than ideological.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A deregulation-friendly Republican objecting purely on separation-of-powers grounds is more persuasive to a court than a partisan objection, strengthening the challenge.
insights.locator: DeLay said he has “sympathy for Carr’s objectives”

insights.claim: The article notes DeLay resigned from Congress in 2006 after a money laundering and conspiracy indictment and was convicted in 2010 before a Texas appeals court overturned it in 2013, context bearing on how much weight his account carries.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Credibility attacks on the intent witness are the obvious counter-move; the substance rests on the statutory text regardless of the messenger.
insights.locator: DeLay left his post as majority leader in September 2005

insights.claim: Former Republican FCC Commissioner Mike O'Rielly independently took the same position, calling the 39 percent cap a statute and not a suggestion and opposing changes under both Democratic and Republican chairmen.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Consistent bipartisan-era Republican agreement that the agency lacks authority undercuts any claim that the repeal reflects settled agency understanding.
insights.quote: I do not believe that the Commission has the authority to modify the national audience reach cap… it is up to Congress to make that determination, not the commission.
insights.locator: Ex-FCC Republican also said FCC can’t change cap

themes.theme: Carr's legal theory and its weak points

insights.claim: Carr's draft argues the FCC can repeal the cap because Congress imposed 39 percent by directing the commission to modify its rules rather than enacting a fixed cap into law, and included no language requiring the level be maintained indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The rule-versus-statute distinction is the entire legal theory; if a court rejects it, the repeal fails and any merger approved under it becomes vulnerable.
insights.locator: Carr’s legal arguments

insights.claim: Carr cites a 2004 3rd Circuit line permitting FCC rule changes outside the context of the quadrennial review, but the author notes the quoted passage refers to defining the UHF discount rather than to setting the cap level.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A mis-anchored precedent citation in the central legal argument is exactly what a reviewing panel latches onto; it materially lowers the odds the repeal survives.
insights.quote: One problem for Carr is that the quoted portion of the court ruling refers to “defining the UHF discount,” not to setting the cap at 39 percent or some other number.
insights.locator: To support this view, Carr quotes a sentence

insights.claim: Carr's strongest support is the Wheeler FCC's 2016 order stating the commission retains authority under the Communications Act to review any aspect of the national audience reach cap and is simply not required to do so during the quadrennial review.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A Democratic FCC's own legal conclusion neutralizes the partisanship framing and is the best asset Carr has on appeal — though Wheeler used it to tighten the cap, not remove it.
insights.quote: no statute bars the Commission from revisiting the cap or the UHF discount
insights.locator: But Carr found backing in the Wheeler FCC’s 2016 order

insights.claim: Carr must clear a higher bar than his predecessors because a 2024 Supreme Court ruling sharply narrowed the leeway agencies get to interpret ambiguous statutes, potentially requiring explicit authority to remove the cap.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The end of broad agency deference cuts against deregulatory as well as regulatory agency action; this is the structural reason to discount the durability of aggressive FCC rulemaking generally.
insights.locator: He may have to show that the FCC has explicit authority

insights.claim: The FCC argues its inability to forbear from enforcing rules against over-cap owners is distinct from its power to alter or eliminate those rules, and adds that forbearance authority does not apply to broadcasters under Title III anyway.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The forbearance argument requires reading a congressional restriction as meaningless surplusage, a construction courts disfavor — another point of vulnerability.
insights.locator: Carr’s proposal claims the forbearance language

themes.theme: UHF discount as the hidden variable

insights.claim: The UHF discount counts only half the households reached by a UHF station toward the cap, so with the discount in place a company owning only UHF stations could reach 78 percent of US households while nominally complying with a 39 percent limit.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The effective cap is already double the nominal one, meaning the practical consolidation headroom that repeal adds is smaller than the 39 percent headline implies.
insights.locator: With the discount in place, a company that only owns UHF stations

insights.claim: The Wheeler FCC eliminated the UHF discount on the reasoning that the digital television transition removed UHF's technical disadvantage and the carveout served only to undermine the cap, but the Pai FCC reversed that a year later and ultimately left both provisions in place.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The whipsaw shows ownership rules flip with each administration; broadcast M&A theses built on a single FCC's posture carry political-cycle risk.
insights.locator: The UHF discount was eliminated just a year earlier

themes.theme: Nexstar-Tegna as the live test case

insights.claim: In March the Carr FCC granted a waiver letting Nexstar Media Group buy Tegna and reach over half of TV households, applying case-by-case treatment before formally adopting it.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The agency is acting as though the rule is already gone, so the repeal vote is partly a retroactive legal shield for a deal already closed — raising the stakes of an adverse court ruling.
insights.locator: Carr already seems to be using the case-by-case approach

insights.claim: Nexstar completed the Tegna acquisition but a federal judge ordered the companies to stop integrating assets and operations, and post-merger integration remains frozen while DirecTV's antitrust suit proceeds.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Closed-but-frozen is the worst state for an acquirer: deal costs incurred, synergies unrealized. It is the concrete downside scenario for anyone underwriting broadcast consolidation on FCC permission alone.
insights.locator: Nexstar completed its acquisition of Tegna

insights.claim: The FCC justified the Nexstar waiver by arguing Congress instructed it to set the cap through rulemaking authority, which necessarily leaves discretion to modify or waive its rules — the same theory underpinning the full repeal.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Shared legal reasoning means one adverse ruling could unwind both the repeal and the waiver, linking the fates of the rule and the deal.
insights.locator: In March, the Carr FCC used the same arguments

insights.claim: The organized opposition is pay-TV distributors, not public-interest groups: the American Television Alliance, whose members include CenturyLink, Charter, Dish, DirecTV, Verizon and USTelecom, says it is confident reviewing courts will quickly overturn the repeal.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The economic driver is retransmission fee leverage — consolidated broadcasters can demand higher carriage fees, so this is a direct margin transfer between broadcasters and distributors.
insights.quote: the commission’s attempt to repeal the broadcast ownership cap ignores Congress’s clear instructions… We are confident that reviewing courts will quickly overturn this misguided action.
insights.locator: TV providers “confident” courts will overrule FCC

insights.claim: Well-funded distributors with standing and an existing litigation posture make a prompt legal challenge near-certain, so the repeal's practical effect depends on whether courts stay it before deals close.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Timing of a stay, not the rulemaking, determines whether broadcast M&A actually moves this cycle — that is the event to watch after Thursday.
insights.locator: A legal challenge could come from TV providers
